reply.question: In simple terms, what does scaled dot-product attention compute, and why divide the query-key dot products by sqrt(d_k)?
reply.text: Scaled dot‑product attention takes a query vector, computes its dot product with each key vector to measure similarity, and then uses those scores (after a softmax) as weights to form a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors [S1][S3]. The dot products are divided by √d_k before the softmax because, when the dimensionality d_k is large, the raw dot products tend to have large magnitude (variance grows with d_k), which pushes the softmax into regions with very small gradients and makes learning difficult [S2]. Scaling by √d_k keeps the magnitude of the scores in a moderate range, preserving stable gradients for the softmax [S2]. This operation can be performed efficiently for many queries at once by packing Q, K, V into matrices and computing softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V [S1].

reply.question: Why use several attention heads instead of one, and what configuration did the paper use?
reply.text:
Multiple attention heads let the model attend to information from different representation subspaces simultaneously, whereas a single head would average over them and lose this diversity [S1].  
The paper therefore employs eight parallel attention heads (h = 8) with each head using dimensions d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64, giving the same overall computational cost as a single full‑dimensional head [S1].

reply.question: How are the positional encodings built, and why sinusoids rather than learned embeddings?
reply.text:
The positional encodings are added to the token embeddings and have the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) so they can be summed; each encoding dimension is a sine or cosine function of the token’s position \(pos\) with wavelengths forming a geometric progression, specifically \(\text{PE}_{(pos,2i)}=\sin\!\big(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big)\) and \(\text{PE}_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos\!\big(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big)\) [S1].  
The authors hypothesized that these sinusoidal functions let the model easily learn relative positions because a fixed offset \(k\) produces a linear transformation of the encoding [S1].  
Experiments showed that learned positional embeddings achieve nearly the same performance as the sinusoidal version [S2][S3].  
However, the sinusoidal scheme was preferred because it can generalize to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, unlike learned embeddings [S3].

reply.question: Per Table 1, how does self-attention compare with recurrent layers on complexity per layer, sequential operations and maximum path length?
reply.text:
According to Table 1, a self‑attention layer has a per‑layer computational complexity of \(O(n^{2}\,d)\) whereas a recurrent layer requires \(O(n\,d^{2})\) [S2].  
Self‑attention needs only a constant number of sequential operations per layer (\(O(1)\)), while a recurrent layer must execute \(O(n)\) sequential operations [S1][S2].  
The maximum path length between any two positions in a self‑attention layer is also constant (\(O(1)\)), in contrast to a recurrent layer where the longest path grows linearly with the sequence length (\(O(n)\)) [S2].

reply.question: Why do the authors say traditional spoken dialogue systems struggle to feel natural?
reply.text: Traditional spoken dialogue systems are built from separate components (voice activity detection, speech recognition, textual dialogue, text‑to‑speech), which creates a latency of several seconds between turns [S1]. Because they convert speech to text, non‑linguistic information such as emotion or non‑speech sounds is discarded, reducing naturalness [S1]. They also enforce a strict speaker‑turn segmentation, preventing the handling of overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections that occur in real conversations [S1].

reply.question: What makes Moshi full-duplex, and how does it handle both sides speaking at once?
reply.text:
Moshi is full‑duplex because it does not rely on a single, turn‑based token stream; instead it models the user’s speech and the system’s speech as two parallel streams of semantic and acoustic tokens that are generated hierarchically in real time[S2][S3].  
By casting spoken dialogue as speech‑to‑speech generation, Moshi can listen and speak simultaneously, removing the need for explicit speaker‑turn segmentation and allowing overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections[S2].  
The architecture uses a text‑language‑model backbone (Helium) together with a residual‑vector‑quantized neural audio codec (Mimi) to produce both streams of tokens in a streaming fashion, so each side’s audio is processed and generated concurrently[S3].  
An “Inner Monologue” component predicts time‑aligned text tokens as a prefix to the audio tokens, which further enables streaming speech recognition while the model is still generating its own speech, supporting continuous bidirectional interaction[S4].  
Thus Moshi’s dual‑stream token generation and hierarchical, time‑aligned processing give it the ability to handle both participants speaking at once with low latency[S3][S4].

reply.question: What is Inner Monologue, and how does it give streaming ASR and TTS?
reply.text: Inner Monologue is a modeling paradigm in Moshi that treats text and audio as parallel token streams and introduces a controllable delay between them, allowing the language model to decide which modality drives generation [S3]. By setting the delay so that audio tokens are delayed relative to text tokens, the model can be forced to predict only text while using ground‑truth audio tokens, which yields a streaming Automatic Speech Recognition system with precise word‑level alignment [S3][S4]. Conversely, when the text tokens are delayed relative to audio tokens, the model generates audio conditioned on the already‑available text, producing a streaming Text‑to‑Speech system [S3][S4]. In practice the same trained Moshi model is used for both tasks; only the delay hyper‑parameter is changed, without any modification to loss, architecture, or training data [S1][S4]. For streaming TTS the audio tokens are delayed by 2 seconds during training, giving the model look‑ahead on text and allowing inference with teacher‑forced text tokens [S1]. For streaming ASR the text tokens are delayed by 2 seconds, letting the model listen to audio before emitting text and inference with teacher‑forced audio tokens [S1].

reply.question: In H-Net, what do the encoder and decoder networks do, and at what resolution do they run?
reply.text:
The encoder network first ingests the raw input, preserves fine‑grained details while compressing the sequence into richer “chunks” that are passed to the main network [S1][S4].  
The decoder network receives the upsampled output of the main network and combines those coarse‑grained representations with the fine‑grained residuals from the encoder to reconstruct information at the original scale [S1][S4].  
Both the encoder and decoder operate on the uncompressed, full‑resolution sequence (i.e., the original resolution before any down‑sampling) [S1][S4].

reply.question: How does H-Net decide where to cut the byte stream into pieces?
reply.text: H‑Net determines chunk boundaries dynamically during inference by using its routing module to decide, for each incoming token, whether the token should be processed by the main network or passed through unchanged, which implicitly selects how many subsequent tokens will be grouped into a chunk [S1]. The model learns to place these boundaries based on statistical regularities in the data; in practice it tends to put cuts at natural linguistic delimiters such as whitespace characters, mirroring the spacelike boundaries used by the SpaceByte tokenizer [S2].

reply.question: Why the ratio loss, and what are F, G and N?
reply.text:
The ratio loss is introduced to steer the model toward a target compression ratio, ensuring that the amount of data retained matches the desired level of compression while still preserving important content [S3].  
In the loss formulation, F denotes the actual fraction of vectors the model keeps, G represents the intended (target) compression fraction, and N is the total number of vectors in the sequence [S3].  
When F equals G, the loss reaches its minimum value of 1 (at F = G = N¹), indicating perfect adherence to the target ratio [S3].  
If F differs from G, the loss can theoretically drop below 1 (e.g., F = N¹+ε and G = N¹−ε), a behavior that is observed during training but still guides the model toward the correct ratio [S3].  
Because the routing module is encouraged to make confident (near‑binary) boundary decisions, F naturally converges toward G, making the ratio loss an effective regularizer for content‑adaptive compression [S3].  
Combined with the autoregressive prediction loss, this mechanism enables the model to learn which vectors to retain based on semantic importance rather than a fixed pattern [S3].
